La cheffe Parveen pétrit la pâte pour le: Chef Parveen kneads the dough for Indian flatbreads. Photo: Edouard Desroches
Exemple de solidarité et d’inclusion, le: A model of solidarity and inclusion, the Curry Collective offers a space where asylum seekers who have just arrived in the country can find their footing in a professional setting by preparing food for low-income people.
Nous sommes un vendredi matin d’avril, l: It’s an April Friday morning, and the soft spring light filters through the windows of the offices of Afrique au Féminin, an organization in the heart of Parc-Extension. This is where we meet Leonora King, project coordinator at Afrique au Féminin, researcher at McGill University and founder of the <l1>Parc-Ex Curry Collective (PECC)</l1>, a community project that employs asylum seekers and women who have recently immigrated to Quebec as chefs.
La jeune femme, élancée et souriante, po: The young woman, slender and smiling, wears a fuchsia pink sweater that suits her cheerful, welcoming personality.
Installée dans ces locaux, Leonora King: Settled in these offices, Leonora King tells us about the beginnings of the PECC, which was born in the middle of the pandemic.
En 2020, Leonora est organisatrice commu: In 2020, Leonora is a community organizer for Afrique au Féminin*, a welcome centre where she leads online workshops. In these workshops, participants passionately share their talents, their music, their dancing and, above all, their recipes.
Dans un large sourire, Léonora partage c: With a broad smile, Leonora shares: “Cooking was popular! The women were proud to share their culinary skills. They took it really seriously. That’s when I thought that maybe they could turn it into a job if I coordinated with my friends.”
Leonora a conscience des obstacles qui s: Leonora is aware of the obstacles these recently arrived women face in Canada, most of whom come from South Asia. “They don’t speak the language and they don’t necessarily have work experience. But I noticed that they are often passionate about cooking,” she explains.
Alors que travailler dans un restaurant: With restaurant work boiling down to delivering meals during the pandemic, Leonora sets up an ordering and delivery system between these women who love to cook and her circle of friends. “They prepared the meals at home, and I took care of delivering the orders,” she sums up.
Cette collaboration se poursuit même apr: The collaboration continues even after restaurants reopen following the lifting of health restrictions. Rather than ending an initiative that is taking off thanks to word of mouth, the Curry Collective eventually moves into the kitchens of Jeunesse au Soleil in 2023. There, the women, now chefs, gather several times a week to prepare orders. Leonora’s role, for its part, hasn’t changed; she picks up the dishes in the late afternoon and delivers them to customers.
Ce qui était à l’origine une initiative: What was originally a temporary initiative to help asylum seekers has now lasted three years, Leonora explains: “I thought I would organize rotations to help other women, but in the end, their number keeps growing.” The condition for these rotations is simple: the chefs must give up their spot at most six months after obtaining permanent residency, so that other women can take over within the Curry Collective.
« Nous avons commencé à six, nous sommes: “We started with six, we are now nine, and we have a waiting list of several interested women,” the young woman reveals in a gloomy tone, aware that she won’t be able to help other women any time soon because of the delays in obtaining permanent residency. She continues: “But I don’t have the heart to ask them to leave. They have become my mothers, my aunts, my sisters,” she tells us, clasping both hands over her heart.
Naila, Parveen, Kamal, Deepali et Promil: Naila, Parveen, Kamal, Deepali and Promila are the chefs of the day. Photo: Edouard Desroches
Dans les cuisines de Jeunesse au Soleil,: In the kitchens of Jeunesse au Soleil, barely a 10-minute walk from the Afrique au Féminin offices, we meet Naila, Parveen, Kamal, Deepali and Promila, the five chefs of the day.
Ces cinq femmes ont toutes commencé cett: All five women began this adventure with Leonora four years ago. Since then, they have never left their positions as chefs, as they are still waiting for their permanent residency.
Il est 11 h, et depuis 8 h, ces femmes s: It is 11 a.m., and since 8 a.m., these women have been busy on site preparing a variety of dishes for an order for more than 200 people. The air is fragrant with delicious smells as the women, focused, go about their tasks.
Elles échangent en hindi, se comprenant: They speak to each other in Hindi, which comes naturally to them. Naila, the most comfortable in English, explains enthusiastically: “What motivates us is working all together and sharing food.”
Lorsque Kamal fait son entrée vers midi,: When Kamal arrives around noon, warm hugs abound. “She’s a chef too,” Naila lets slip with a knowing smile.
« Nous sommes des cheffes, car nous avon: “We are chefs because we have always cooked at home. It’s a passion we have completely mastered,” says Deepali before hugging Kamal in turn, then going back to cooking the Indian flatbreads.
<strong>« Sans le Collectif de Curry, no: “Without the Curry Collective, we would still be unemployed”
Dans l’effervescence de la cuisine, Nail: In the bustle of the kitchen, Naila carefully chops vegetables to go with the spiced rice and chicken she has already prepared, all while answering our questions. One striking detail emerges from her answers and confirms what Leonora said: Naila, like all the women working around her, has never worked before.
La cheffe Naila dans la cuisine de Jeune: Chef Naila in the kitchen of Jeunesse au Soleil. Photo: Edouard Desroches
« Je me suis mariée il y a 10 ans et je: “I got married 10 years ago and I never worked anywhere but at home as a housewife,” she confides. In early 2020, while pregnant with her second daughter, Naila left her first host country, Saudi Arabia, with her husband and eldest daughter. Their goal is clear: to give their daughters a different future, one in which they can choose their own career path.
« S’il n’y avait pas le Collectif de Cur: “If there were no Curry Collective, we would all still be unemployed,” Naila says, as the other chefs nod in agreement, recognizing how lucky they are to have had this opportunity.
Ici, au sein du Collectif de Curry, leur: Here, within the Curry Collective, their culinary skills are recognized, the language barrier doesn’t exist, and it is possible to balance work and family life.
Chacune travaille de manière équitable e: Each of them works an equal share, between 5 and 15 hours a week, an ideal compromise for them. Naila continues: “It’s not a lot, but we are happy, because most of us have young children. Working all day isn’t possible for us. But if we had more orders, we would be just as happy, because I know we could organize ourselves.”
Naila ajoute qu’elle peut maintenant dép: Naila adds that she can now drop her two daughters, aged seven and four, off at school, go to work, then pick them up before the end of the day, which wasn’t the case less than a year ago. “Even last year, we didn’t have access to subsidized daycare, which made looking for a job impossible,” she explains.
Parveen, qui est âgée de 71 ans, est la: Parveen, who is 71, is the eldest of the group. Affectionately called “grandma,” she shows remarkable manual dexterity. In the space of three hours, she has managed to prepare around a hundred Maggi Balls, fried potato dumplings, and is now kneading the dough for the flatbreads that Deepali cooks. Naila acts as Parveen’s interpreter: “At my age, without the Curry Collective, it would have been impossible to find any job at all.”
Parc-Extension est un lieu emblématique: Parc-Extension is an emblematic hub of South Asian culture. Accordingly, the women of the Curry Collective are mainly of Indian and Pakistani origin. Leonora, however, is considering opening the kitchens to women from other parts of the world.
Elle explique : « Il y a des demandeuses: She explains: “There are asylum seekers from different backgrounds who need work. I think it’s a richness to taste dishes cooked by women from those countries, who have mastered the authentic recipes and can share them with others. We could consider Mexican, Togolese or other world cuisines...” She raises the possibility with a touch of reverie, before adding: “But it will depend on our financial resources... For now, we can’t afford to hire more women,” she concludes with an awkward smile.
*Afrique au Féminin : Créé en 1986 à l'o: *Afrique au Féminin: Founded in 1986 to support immigrant women of African origin, Afrique au Féminin expanded its work to welcome women of all backgrounds when it obtained offices in Montréal’s Parc-Extension neighbourhood in 1990, an area where the South Asian population is the majority.
